q: A 27-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on haloperidol 10 mg/day for 3 months and his hallucinations have resolved. His family now reports that he is withdrawn, speaks very little, has a flat face and has stopped bathing. Examination shows normal tone, no tremor, normal gait with arm swing, no akathisia and no galactorrhoea. Which explanation and change in treatment are most appropriate?
o: Excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway; increase the haloperidol dose
D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway; add an anticholinergic such as trihexyphenidyl
D2 blockade in the mesocortical pathway; switch to a second-generation (5-HT2A/D2) antipsychotic
D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway; add bromocriptine
e: Typical antipsychotics block D2 receptors in all four pathways. Blocking the already hypodopaminergic mesocortical pathway worsens (secondary) negative symptoms; second-generation drugs with 5-HT2A antagonism raise cortical dopamine and are preferred. Nigrostriatal blockade would show rigidity, tremor or bradykinesia (excluded here); tuberoinfundibular blockade gives hyperprolactinaemia; mesolimbic dopamine is already controlled, as the hallucinations resolved.

q: A 36-year-old woman with bipolar disorder has been stable for 3 years on lithium (level 0.7 mEq/L). Two weeks after a new antihypertensive was added she develops coarse tremor, vomiting, ataxia and polyuria; serum lithium is 2.3 mEq/L and creatinine is unchanged. Which drug most likely caused this, and by what mechanism?
o: Amlodipine, by inhibiting tubular secretion of lithium
Atenolol, by reducing hepatic metabolism of lithium
Prazosin, by displacing lithium from plasma proteins
Hydrochlorothiazide, by sodium depletion that increases proximal tubular lithium reabsorption
e: Lithium is handled like sodium: filtered, then largely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. Thiazides (also ACE inhibitors, ARBs and NSAIDs) cause sodium/volume depletion, increasing proximal reabsorption and raising lithium levels by roughly 25-40%. Lithium is neither protein-bound nor hepatically metabolised, so options B and C are mechanistically wrong; calcium-channel blockers are not recognised to raise levels.

q: A 52-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis (ascites, bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, INR 1.9) is brought 40 hours after his last drink with coarse tremor, sweating, anxiety and vivid visual hallucinations. He is fully oriented; pulse 112/min, random blood glucose 62 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Parenteral thiamine first, then IV dextrose, with lorazepam for withdrawal
Oral chlordiazepoxide followed by IV dextrose
IV dextrose followed by parenteral thiamine, with lorazepam for withdrawal
IV haloperidol for the hallucinations with prophylactic phenytoin
e: Hallucinations with a clear sensorium at 12-48 h = alcoholic hallucinosis (withdrawal). In severe hepatic impairment use benzodiazepines cleared by glucuronidation without active metabolites (lorazepam, oxazepam); chlordiazepoxide and diazepam accumulate. Thiamine must precede glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold, and phenytoin does not prevent withdrawal seizures.

q: A 20-year-old student is brought to the emergency room with sudden bilateral loss of vision on the morning of her final practical examination. She seems curiously unconcerned. Pupils are equal and briskly reactive, fundi are normal, optokinetic nystagmus is present and visual evoked potentials are normal. She cannot explain the symptom and no one has seen her feign other problems. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Anton syndrome
Conversion (functional neurological symptom) disorder
Malingering
Factitious disorder
e: Objectively intact visual pathways (pupils, OKN, VEP) with abrupt loss in a stressful setting and 'la belle indifference' point to conversion disorder: the symptom is not consciously produced and relieves anxiety (primary gain). Anton syndrome is cortical blindness with denial and absent OKN; malingering requires conscious feigning for an external goal; factitious disorder requires deliberate production to assume the sick role.

q: A 23-year-old woman with a BMI of 22 kg/m2 reports secret episodes of eating large amounts followed by self-induced vomiting 4-5 times a week for 8 months. Examination: bilateral parotid enlargement, calluses on the back of the hand, dental enamel erosion. Labs: K+ 2.9 mEq/L, HCO3- 34 mEq/L, Cl- 88 mEq/L. Which drug is most appropriate to add to cognitive behavioural therapy?
o: Fluoxetine
Bupropion
Olanzapine
Lithium
e: Normal weight with binge-purge behaviour, Russell's sign, parotid swelling and hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis = bulimia nervosa. CBT plus an SSRI (fluoxetine, higher dose around 60 mg/day) is first-line. Bupropion is contraindicated (seizure risk with purging and electrolyte disturbance). Olanzapine is used in anorexia nervosa; lithium has no role.

q: A 31-year-old man on haloperidol 20 mg/day for acute psychosis develops, over 3 days, a temperature of 40.1 C, generalised lead-pipe rigidity, fluctuating consciousness, labile blood pressure and CPK of 14,000 U/L. Reflexes are normal to reduced and there is no clonus. After stopping haloperidol and starting cooling and fluids, which drug is the most appropriate specific treatment?
o: Cyproheptadine
Benztropine
Dantrolene
Propranolol
e: Slow onset, lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability and raised CPK after a dopamine antagonist = neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Dantrolene (muscle relaxant; bromocriptine is the dopamine-agonist alternative) is specific therapy. Cyproheptadine is for serotonin syndrome (rapid onset, clonus, hyperreflexia); anticholinergics such as benztropine can worsen hyperthermia; propranolol is not recommended.

q: A 60-kg man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after a house fire. He has blistered, weeping, painful burns over the entire front of the trunk, the whole left upper limb and the anterior surface of the right lower limb; the face shows only erythema without blisters. No fluids were given before arrival. Using the Parkland formula, what hourly rate of Ringer lactate should be run for the next 6 hours?
o: 360 mL/h
540 mL/h
720 mL/h
e: TBSA (second/third-degree only) by rule of nines: front of trunk 18% + left arm 9% + anterior right leg 9% = 36%; facial erythema (first degree) is excluded. Parkland: 4 mL x 60 kg x 36 = 8,640 mL/24 h; half (4,320 mL) in the first 8 h counted from the time of injury. Two hours have elapsed, so 4,320 mL over the remaining 6 h = 720 mL/h. 540 uses 8 h; 1,080 ignores halving; 360 spreads 24 h evenly. Titrate to urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/h.

q: A 64-year-old man has progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids for 4 months with a 9-kg weight loss. A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophageal body with smooth tapering at the lower end (bird's beak). Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Pneumatic balloon dilatation
Laparoscopic Heller myotomy with Dor fundoplication
Botulinum toxin injection at the lower oesophageal sphincter
Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy and cross-sectional imaging or EUS
e: A short history (under 6 months), age over 50 and marked weight loss with a beak-like lower oesophagus raise suspicion of pseudoachalasia (usually a gastro-oesophageal junction carcinoma infiltrating the plexus), which mimics achalasia on barium and manometry. Malignancy must be excluded by endoscopy with biopsy and EUS/CT before any achalasia therapy (balloon, myotomy or toxin).

q: Three weeks after a laparoscopic TEP mesh repair of a right inguinal hernia, a man complains of burning pain and numbness over the anterolateral aspect of the right thigh, worse on standing. The operation note records that a tacker was used to fix the mesh. Where was the tack most likely placed?
o: Lateral to the gonadal vessels and below the iliopubic tract (triangle of pain)
Between the vas deferens and the gonadal vessels (triangle of doom)
Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels within Hesselbach's triangle
Over the corona mortis near the superior pubic ramus
e: Anterolateral thigh paraesthesia is lateral femoral cutaneous nerve territory. The triangle of pain (lateral to the gonadal vessels, below the iliopubic tract) contains the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve, so fixation there is avoided. The triangle of doom (between vas and gonadal vessels) holds the external iliac vessels; Hesselbach's triangle and the corona mortis carry no relevant nerve (vascular risk instead).

q: After a modified radical mastectomy with axillary clearance, a woman cannot raise her right arm fully overhead and the medial border of the scapula protrudes when she pushes against a wall. She also reports numbness of the skin of the upper medial arm and axilla. Which nerves were injured?
o: Long thoracic and thoracodorsal nerves
Long thoracic and intercostobrachial nerves
Thoracodorsal and medial pectoral nerves
Dorsal scapular and intercostobrachial nerves
e: Winging of the scapula (serratus anterior paralysis) = long thoracic nerve, which runs on the chest wall in the axilla; the intercostobrachial nerve (T2) supplies the skin of the axilla and upper medial arm and is commonly divided. Thoracodorsal injury weakens latissimus dorsi (adduction, internal rotation, extension) without winging; the dorsal scapular nerve lies in the neck and is not at risk in axillary clearance.

q: A 38-year-old euthyroid woman has a solitary 3-cm thyroid nodule. FNAC shows a cellular smear with microfollicular architecture, scant colloid and no papillary nuclear features. What is the best next step?
o: Total thyroidectomy
Repeat FNAC after 6 weeks
Diagnostic hemithyroidectomy with histopathology
Radioiodine ablation
e: This is a follicular neoplasm (Bethesda IV). FNAC cannot distinguish follicular adenoma from carcinoma, which requires capsular or vascular invasion on histology, so diagnostic lobectomy is indicated, with completion surgery if carcinoma is found. Repeat FNAC suits non-diagnostic or AUS/FLUS (Bethesda III) smears; total thyroidectomy and radioiodine are premature.

q: A 24-year-old man is brought after a road traffic accident with blood pressure 128/82 mmHg and pulse 88/min. FAST shows fluid in the splenorenal space. CECT abdomen: grade III splenic laceration without contrast blush; no other injury. What is the best management?
o: Non-operative management with close monitoring, serial haemoglobin and angio-embolisation if a blush or instability develops
Emergency splenectomy
Splenorrhaphy within the first 6 hours
Diagnostic peritoneal lavage
e: A haemodynamically stable blunt splenic injury, even with positive FAST and a moderate-grade laceration, is managed non-operatively in a monitored setting; angio-embolisation is added for contrast blush and surgery only for instability or failure. FAST and DPL are triage tools in unstable patients, not reasons to operate on a stable one.

q: A primigravida with severe preeclampsia is on the Pritchard regimen of magnesium sulphate. Four hours after the loading dose a maintenance dose is due. Her respiratory rate is 18/min, patellar reflexes are brisk, and she has passed 70 mL of urine over the previous 4 hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the scheduled maintenance dose because reflexes and respiration are normal
Withhold the dose, check serum magnesium and reassess
Give 10% calcium gluconate IV and stop all further doses
Halve the next dose and continue
e: Pritchard's checks before each maintenance dose: patellar reflex present, respiratory rate 16/min or more, and urine output at least 30 mL/h (100 mL in 4 h). Magnesium is renally excreted, so low urine output predicts accumulation before reflexes or respiration fail. Withhold the dose, check serum magnesium (therapeutic 4-7 mEq/L) and reassess. Calcium gluconate is for established toxicity (loss of reflexes, respiratory depression).

q: A 34-year-old woman with chronic hypertension (BP 164/104 mmHg before delivery) and bronchial asthma has an atonic postpartum haemorrhage after a vaginal delivery. Uterine massage, oxytocin 10 IU IM and an oxytocin infusion have failed; blood loss is 1,200 mL and ongoing. Which uterotonic is the most appropriate next?
o: Methylergometrine 0.2 mg IM
Carboprost 250 microgram IM
Misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual
Oxytocin 10 IU undiluted rapid IV bolus
e: Methylergometrine causes vasoconstriction and is contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia; carboprost (15-methyl PGF2 alpha) causes bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma; a rapid undiluted IV oxytocin bolus causes hypotension and arrhythmias. Misoprostol (PGE1) 800 microgram sublingual has none of these restrictions.

q: A 30-year-old Rh-negative G3P2 with a previous hydropic stillbirth has an indirect Coombs titre of 1:64 at 26 weeks. Which is the best next test to assess for fetal anaemia?
o: Amniotic fluid optical density (delta OD450) measurement
Kleihauer-Betke test on maternal blood
Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling
Doppler measurement of the fetal middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity
e: A titre above the critical level (1:16 or more) in a sensitised mother needs surveillance for fetal anaemia. MCA peak systolic velocity above 1.5 MoM is a non-invasive, accurate predictor of moderate-severe anaemia and has replaced delta OD450 (invasive, less accurate). Cordocentesis is reserved for confirmation and intrauterine transfusion; Kleihauer-Betke quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage for anti-D dosing.

q: A 26-year-old woman at 22 weeks of gestation with a known 8-cm intramural fibroid presents with 2 days of severe localised abdominal pain over the fibroid, vomiting and a temperature of 37.9 C. WBC is 13,500/microL, fetal heart rate is normal, and there are no contractions or bleeding. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous mass at the site of tenderness with no fluid collection. What is the best management?
o: Conservative: rest, hydration and analgesia with observation
Emergency myomectomy
Tocolysis with nifedipine and antenatal steroids
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for suspected infection of the fibroid
e: Red (carneous) degeneration typically occurs in large fibroids in the second trimester: acute localised pain, low-grade fever, leucocytosis and vomiting without labour or infection. Management is conservative (rest, hydration, analgesia, observation); surgery or antibiotics are not needed, and tocolysis is unnecessary without contractions.

q: A 36-week primigravida is admitted with spontaneous rupture of membranes. Within seconds she passes bright red blood per vagina; she is haemodynamically stable and the uterus is soft and non-tender. CTG now shows a sinusoidal pattern with a fetal heart rate of 90/min. What is the most likely diagnosis and best immediate action?
o: Abruptio placentae; expectant management
Placenta previa; expectant management
Uterine rupture; laparotomy after resuscitation
Vasa previa (Benckiser haemorrhage); emergency caesarean section
e: Bleeding that starts with membrane rupture, a stable mother and rapid fetal compromise (sinusoidal or bradycardic CTG) indicates rupture of fetal vessels running in the membranes (vasa previa); the baby is bleeding, so immediate caesarean section. Abruption is painful with a tense uterus; placenta previa bleeds are maternal and usually precede rupture; the Apt-Downey test can confirm fetal haemoglobin if time allows.

q: A 35-year-old G4P3L3 with three previous caesarean sections has an anterior placenta previa at 31 weeks. Doppler ultrasound shows loss of the retroplacental clear zone, multiple vascular lacunae and bridging vessels toward the bladder. What is the best management plan?
o: Induce labour at 37 weeks, then manual removal of the placenta
Planned caesarean at 34-36 weeks with the placenta left in situ, followed by hysterectomy, in a centre with blood bank and ICU support
Await spontaneous labour with oxytocin augmentation
Elective caesarean at 39 weeks with controlled cord traction
e: Prior caesareans plus anterior previa and these imaging signs = placenta accreta spectrum. Attempting to separate or pull the placenta causes torrential haemorrhage. The standard is a multidisciplinary, planned preterm (34-36 weeks) caesarean, delivering the baby through an incision away from the placenta, and hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ.

q: A charred body is recovered from a burnt-down house. The pathologist is asked to decide whether the person was alive when the fire started. Which finding best supports this?
o: Pugilistic (boxer's) attitude of the limbs
Extradural collection of chocolate-brown, friable blood (heat haematoma)
Soot in the trachea and bronchi below the vocal cords with raised blood carboxyhaemoglobin
Splitting of the skin along the joints and flexures
e: Soot inhaled into the lower airways and raised COHb show that the person breathed during the fire. Pugilistic posture (heat stiffening), skin splitting (heat rupture) and heat haematoma are post-mortem artefacts caused by heat acting on the body and do not prove life at the time of the fire.

q: A badly putrefied body is recovered from a river ten days after the person went missing. External signs such as froth, cutis anserina and washerwoman's hands are no longer evaluable. Which investigation is most useful to support antemortem drowning?
o: Gettler's test comparing chloride content of left and right heart blood
Demonstration of diatoms in the bone marrow of a long bone
Specific gravity of blood from the heart chambers
Weight and frothy fluid of the lungs on gross examination
e: Diatoms inhaled during drowning enter the circulation and lodge in closed organs such as bone marrow, which is protected from putrefaction and contamination, so the bone-marrow diatom test works in decomposed bodies. Gettler's test and blood specific gravity are unreliable (especially after putrefaction or in sea water), and lung and external findings are lost with decomposition.

q: A farmer treated with atropine and pralidoxime for organophosphate poisoning recovers from his cholinergic crisis. On day 3 he cannot lift his head from the pillow and has proximal limb weakness, ptosis and shallow breathing. Pupils are not constricted and there is no sweating, salivation or bradycardia. Which statement is correct?
o: Organophosphate-induced delayed polyneuropathy from neuropathy target esterase inhibition; distal weakness appears after 2-3 weeks
Relapse of the cholinergic crisis; needs higher doses of atropine
Guillain-Barre syndrome; needs IV immunoglobulin
Intermediate syndrome from persistent neuromuscular cholinesterase inhibition; needs ventilatory support, not more atropine or oximes
e: Onset 24-96 h after the acute phase with neck-flexor, proximal limb, cranial nerve and respiratory muscle weakness but no muscarinic features = intermediate syndrome. Atropine and oximes do not reverse it; management is respiratory support, with recovery in 5-18 days. OPIDN is distal and appears at 1-3 weeks.

q: Four assault victims are examined by the medical officer. Whose injury qualifies as 'grievous hurt' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
o: A man with a 5-cm sutured scalp laceration discharged the next day
A man with a fracture of one rib on chest radiograph
A woman with multiple forearm bruises who could not do her usual work for 12 days
A man whose scalp hair was forcibly cut off with a razor
e: Grievous hurt includes emasculation, permanent loss of sight or hearing, privation or permanent impairment of a limb or joint, permanent disfigurement of head or face, fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth, and hurt that endangers life or leaves the victim in severe pain or unable to follow ordinary pursuits for 20 days. A fracture qualifies; a sutured laceration, 12 days of disability and loss of hair (not permanent disfigurement) are simple hurt.

q: A 28-year-old farmer who slept on the floor wakes with mild periumbilical pain, drooping eyelids and difficulty swallowing. There is a tiny bite mark on the foot, no swelling or bleeding, and the 20-minute whole blood clotting test is normal. What is the most likely snake and the most important step?
o: Common krait; start polyvalent anti-snake venom early and prepare for ventilatory support
Russell's viper; start ASV only if the 20WBCT turns abnormal
Saw-scaled viper; give ASV with fresh frozen plasma
Common cobra; observe for local necrosis before deciding on ASV
e: A painless nocturnal bite in someone sleeping on the floor, minimal local signs, abdominal pain, ptosis and bulbar weakness with a normal 20WBCT = neurotoxic envenomation by the common krait. Early polyvalent ASV and airway/ventilation readiness are key (a neostigmine-atropine trial helps only postsynaptic blockade). Vipers cause local swelling and coagulopathy (abnormal 20WBCT); cobra bites usually cause marked local necrosis.

q: A young woman's body is found with a continuous horizontal ligature mark encircling the neck at the level of the thyroid cartilage, a fractured hyoid bone, bruising of the strap muscles, facial congestion and conjunctival petechiae. There is no suspension point. The most likely cause of death is:
o: Typical suicidal hanging
Throttling (manual strangulation)
Ligature strangulation
Smothering
e: A horizontal, complete, deep ligature mark at or below the thyroid cartilage with hyoid or cartilage fractures and strap-muscle bruising indicates ligature strangulation (usually homicidal). In hanging the mark is oblique, incomplete (gap at the knot) and above the thyroid cartilage; throttling shows crescentic nail marks and finger bruises; smothering leaves mouth and nose injuries.

q: A 40-year-old woman on fluoxetine is given tramadol for pain. Within 8 hours she develops agitation, tremor, sweating, diarrhoea, a temperature of 39 C, hyperreflexia and inducible ankle clonus; muscle tone is only mildly increased. After stopping both drugs and giving benzodiazepines, which drug is most appropriate if symptoms persist?
o: Dantrolene
Bromocriptine
Cyproheptadine
Propranolol
e: Rapid onset (under 24 h), hyperreflexia, inducible clonus, diarrhoea and mild hypertonia after combining an SSRI with tramadol = serotonin syndrome. Cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) is the antidote used. Dantrolene and bromocriptine are for NMS (bromocriptine may worsen serotonin toxicity); propranolol can mask tachycardia and worsen hyperthermia.

q: A 26-year-old woman beginning HRZE therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis wants a reliable contraceptive for the next three years without daily reminders. Which method retains full efficacy during rifampicin therapy?
o: Combined oral contraceptive pill with 30 microgram ethinylestradiol
Progestin-only pill
Etonogestrel subdermal implant
Copper intrauterine device
e: Rifampicin is a potent CYP3A4 (and UGT) inducer that lowers oestrogen and progestin levels, so combined pills, progestin-only pills and implants may fail (MEC category 3). The copper IUD does not depend on hepatic metabolism and is unaffected (as are DMPA and LNG-IUS).

q: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with Kussmaul breathing, pH 7.08, glucose 520 mg/dL, positive ketones and serum potassium 2.9 mEq/L. After 1 L of normal saline, which step is correct?
o: Start a regular insulin infusion at 0.1 U/kg/h immediately and add potassium later
Withhold insulin and give IV potassium until K+ is 3.3 mEq/L or more, then start insulin
Give sodium bicarbonate 100 mEq to correct acidosis before insulin
Start insulin and add potassium only when serum K+ exceeds 5 mEq/L
e: Insulin drives potassium into cells; starting it at K+ below 3.3 mEq/L can precipitate fatal arrhythmias and respiratory muscle weakness, and total body potassium is already depleted despite acidosis. Replace potassium (20-30 mEq/h with monitoring) until above 3.3, then start insulin and keep K+ at 4-5 mEq/L. Bicarbonate is reserved for pH below 6.9.

q: A 66-year-old man with heart failure receives two units of packed red cells for anaemia. During the second unit he develops breathlessness, hypertension, distended neck veins, bilateral crepitations and a raised BNP. He is afebrile and improves with furosemide. Which reaction is most likely?
o: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
Transfusion-related acute lung injury
Febrile non-haemolytic reaction
Anaphylactic reaction due to anti-IgA antibodies
e: Pulmonary oedema with hypertension, raised JVP, raised BNP and response to diuretics indicates volume overload (TACO). TRALI causes hypotension, fever, normal or low BNP and no diuretic response; FNHTR gives fever and chills without respiratory failure; anaphylaxis gives bronchospasm, urticaria and hypotension.

q: The annual incidence of lung cancer is 30 per 1,000 among smokers and 10 per 1,000 among non-smokers. If 20% of the population smokes, what proportion of lung cancer cases in the whole population is attributable to smoking?
e: Incidence in the total population = 0.2 x 30 + 0.8 x 10 = 14 per 1,000. Population attributable risk = 14 - 10 = 4 per 1,000, so PAR% = 4/14 = 28.6%. 66.7% is the attributable risk % among the exposed (20/30); 40% is PAR relative to the unexposed rate (4/10); 20% is merely the prevalence of smoking.

q: A 9-year-old boy in a long-arm plaster cast for a supracondylar humerus fracture reduced 12 hours earlier cries with increasing forearm pain not relieved by analgesics. Passive extension of the fingers is intensely painful. The radial pulse is palpable and capillary refill is normal. What is the next step?
o: Elevate the arm above heart level and give stronger analgesia
Urgent arteriography
Remove or split the cast and padding down to the skin, then reassess
Immediate forearm fasciotomy
e: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs of compartment syndrome; pulses and capillary refill are late and may stay normal. First release all circumferential constriction (split cast and padding) and keep the limb at heart level (elevation lowers perfusion pressure); fasciotomy follows if there is no improvement.

q: During a supraclavicular brachial plexus block in a 60-kg patient, 40 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine is injected. Within minutes the patient reports perioral numbness, a metallic taste and tinnitus, then has a generalised seizure followed by hypotension and a widened QRS complex. Apart from airway support and seizure control with a benzodiazepine, what is the most specific treatment?
o: Epinephrine 1 mg IV bolus
Amiodarone 300 mg IV
Phenytoin loading dose
20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus followed by infusion
e: Circumoral numbness and tinnitus, then seizures and cardiovascular collapse after a large dose (200 mg, about 3.3 mg/kg, above the 2-2.5 mg/kg limit) = local anaesthetic systemic toxicity. Lipid emulsion (bolus then infusion) is the specific antidote; if arrest occurs use small epinephrine doses (1 microgram/kg or less), avoid vasopressin and continue CPR. Phenytoin is ineffective for LAST seizures; amiodarone is only an alternative for ventricular arrhythmia.
